Paul writes to the Christians of Colossae, whom he probably did not know personally. He speaks to them about Christ, in whom are "all the treasures of wisdom." His concern is that some were teaching ideas that drew people away from Christ. The Bible does not spell out here exactly what those ideas were, and scholars debate their origin. Paul wants their faith to remain firm.

Today, before accepting a teaching that sounds very convincing, ask yourself: does it bring me closer to Christ, and does it agree with what the Scriptures say? Studying the Bible with other believers helps us avoid being carried away merely by the attractiveness of a speech.
exp.2:21:
The explanation says that servants (slaves) were to obey their earthly masters in everything. "Human masters" means masters of flesh, of this world. Working only when someone is watching you, in order to look good before people, is what the verse calls "eyeservice". Instead, they should serve with a whole heart, that is, with sincerity, and with reverence toward God.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Colossae, and in this passage he gives instructions to different members of the household. Slavery was common in the Roman world at that time. Paul neither approves of nor condemns it here; he speaks to believers who lived within that reality and shows them how to live out their faith. Some scholars think this planted ideas that later would challenge that system.

For today: work honestly even when no one is watching you, knowing that God does see. Do your work with sincerity, as an act of respect toward Him.
exp.2:17:
Paul asks wives to submit to their husbands. Submitting means willingly placing oneself under the husband's leadership, and the phrase "as it is fit in the Lord" indicates that this should be done as part of living for Christ.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Colossae, probably while he is in prison. After speaking of a life filled with the word of Christ, he gives instructions for the home: to wives, husbands, and children. In the ancient world this was common, but Paul places it "in the Lord" and also requires love and tenderness from husbands. Christians understand the scope of this submission in different ways.

For today: in marriage, let both seek to honor Christ with respect, dialogue, and love. Before a disagreement, pray together and ask: "How can we please the Lord in this?"
exp.2:14:
This verse says that the peace that comes from God should "rule" in our hearts, meaning it should be the one that decides and guides us when there is tension or doubt. That peace is something God has called us to as part of one body, the church. It ends with an invitation: "be ye thankful."

The writer is the apostle Paul, addressing the believers in Colossae. He has just asked them for patience, forgiveness, and love toward one another, as Christ forgave them. That is why peace is not only a personal feeling but something that unites the community. Afterward, Paul speaks of the word of Christ, the singing, and gratitude.

For today: before you respond in a family disagreement or at church, pause and pray. Ask yourself which decision keeps peace and forgiveness alive. Then thank God for something concrete about that person.

sum.2: Paul teaches that since believers have been raised with Christ, they should set their minds on the things above and leave behind sin, such as sexual immorality, greed, anger, and lying. They should clothe themselves with compassion, humility, forgiveness, and love, letting the peace and the word of Christ guide their lives. He also gives instructions to husbands, children, parents, and servants, so that they do everything for the Lord.
sum.0: Paul gives thanks to God for the faith, love, and hope of the believers in Colossae, and he prays that they will grow in wisdom and bear fruit. He teaches that Jesus is the image of the invisible God, the Creator and the head of the church, and that through his cross he reconciles us to God. Paul serves the church and proclaims Christ, the hope of glory.
sum.3: Paul encourages believers to pray steadily and with thankfulness, to treat their servants fairly, and to live wisely and speak graciously to those who do not believe. He then sends greetings from his companions, including Tychicus, Onesimus, Mark, Epaphras, and Luke, asks that the letter also be read in Laodicea, and urges Archippus to carry out the ministry he has received.
sum.1: Paul shows how deeply he cares about the believers in Colossae and Laodicea, and he warns them not to be taken in by human philosophies. He reminds them that all the fullness of God dwells in Christ, that through Him they were forgiven and raised to new life, and that they no longer need to submit to religious rules made by people.
